title: Fatimah al-Fihri's Qarawiyyin
hookLine: a woman in Fez spends her inheritance on a mosque that becomes a place of learning

lines: IT WON'T STAY ONLY A MOSQUE.
cards: An inheritance arrives. A father has died, and his daughter now has money of her own. A house, a business, a cushion for bad years?

In Fez, in Morocco, a woman named Fatimah al-Fihri, whose family had come to the city from Kairouan, the chronicle says, chose a mosque. It would become the Qarawiyyin, and it would not stay only a mosque.
The path crosses the strait to North Africa.

teach.b: Much of the story comes from a later chronicle of Fez, which tells it simply. Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad al-Fihri, was a devout woman. She spent what she inherited on building the mosque, from the ground up.
Tradition adds that she fasted the whole time the building went on. And the chronicle says her sister Maryam did the same across the river, building a mosque for the other half of the city.
Two sisters, two inheritances, two mosques. Why would someone do this? A hadith fits her story.
Sahih Muslim records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in substance: when a person dies, their deeds end except for three things.
Knowledge people go on benefiting from. A good child who prays for them. Fatimah's mosque became the first two at once.
Prayer filled it, and then teaching did. Scholars taught the Qur'an, law, grammar, and later much more, and students came from far away to sit in its circles.
Over time it grew into what Fez now calls the University of al-Qarawiyyin. So the line isn't an exaggeration, just a long view.

Look back over this week, and it's full of builders: a jurist who wrote on love, a judge who defended reason, a mystic, neighbors who built a shared and fragile culture, a palace that credited God with every win, a people who kept faith in hiding.
And now a daughter with an inheritance.

how: The Qarawiyyin in Fez is still a working mosque and a center of Islamic learning, and Muslims often cite Fatimah al-Fihri as an example of charity that keeps giving.

o: a family of scholars who came to Fez from Kairouan
the mosque in Fez that grew into a university
the river that splits Fez into two halves

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: built the mosque with her inheritance
her sister, who built another mosque

s: the Qarawiyyin was founded by a king
the chronicle says Fatimah al-Fihri built it with what she inherited.
teaching circles grew in it, and over time it became a university.
Fatimah was the only sister who built a mosque

games.q: you're Fatimah al-Fihri in Fez. your father has died, and you've inherited wealth of your own. what do you do with it?
o: keep it safe for hard years.
build a mosque for your neighborhood.
give it all to the ruler of the city.
games.why: she built a mosque, and teaching circles grew inside it until it became a university.

practice: Bring one woman to mind who started something that outlasted the moment: a grandmother who began a family tradition, a teacher who started a reading club, a neighbor who organized the food drive.
Picture what she built, and who is still benefiting from it. If you pray, remember her in your prayer; if you don't, hold her name with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Qarawiyyin. The mosque Fatimah al-Fihri built in Fez with her inheritance, which grew into a university. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: flowing charity, the gift whose good keeps running after the giver is gone.

carryVoice: Your line: she founded a university. What she began is still flowing. Day nine hundred forty-five, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Abi Zar', Rawd al-Qirtas (Fatimah al-Fihri builds the Qarawiyyin; her sister Maryam builds the Andalusian mosque)
Sahih Muslim 1631 (deeds end except three: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, a righteous child who prays)
